name: Chloe Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying animal science, so it's mostly biology, nutrition and some farm management. Mornings are lectures, afternoons I'm either at the university farm or in the library, and twice a week I do reception shifts at a vet clinic. I share a flat with two girls from my course who are as animal-mad as I am. My family has a farm, sheep and some arable, about ninety minutes from here, and I go home every second weekend.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the university farm mornings, when the frost is on the grass and the lambs are making a racket. What wears me out is that I try to be good at everything and still call home to check how lambing is going. And that my brother and I both want the farm, and we haven't discussed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing dramatic, and I'd say farming has always seen new tools come and go. I'd tell my friends that the tools I use already, for rations and flock records, are plenty good enough. I'd also say prices and weather are still the real boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit uneasy, because the farm isn't making much anyway. Feed prices are up and lamb prices are flat, so Dad's margin is thin, and neither AI nor the lack of it changes that. And I'd wonder whether the farm is big enough for both me and my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd use my AI tools for study and for the vet clinic's booking system, like I already do. I'd keep my reception shifts and save fifty pounds a month. And I'd start a spreadsheet of the farm's costs on the weekends I'm home, because I think there's money we're losing in feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, steady, but with the farm worry in the back of my head like a stone in a boot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the farm's money situation affect your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Does the farm's money situation affect your degree?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI tools for the flock records?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Dad pays my rent, and I know it hurts. If a hard year came, I'd be the first thing he'd cut. So I want to be useful, not just a cost. If I can find savings in the feed bill, that pays for my degree three times over.

say: I'd say **nothing dramatic**: farming has always seen new tools come and go.
I'd tell friends **prices and weather** are still the real boss.
think: The farm's **margin is thin**, and neither AI nor its absence changes that.
I wonder whether the farm is big enough for **me and my brother**.
do: **Keep** using AI tools for study and the vet clinic's booking system.
**Save** fifty pounds a month and keep my reception shifts.
**Build** a spreadsheet of the farm's costs on my weekends home.
feel: **Steady**, with the farm worry like a stone in a boot.
S0.quote: If I can find savings in the feed bill, that pays for my degree three times over.
fieldNote: Chloe's **unease** is about the **farm**: thin margins and a succession question with her brother.
She uses AI tools **already** and treats them as normal equipment.
She wants to be **useful**, not a cost, which shapes her plans.

steps.text: Keep the two weekly vet clinic reception shifts
Save fifty pounds a month from reception pay
Build a spreadsheet of the farm's feed costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good news for anyone who works with it, and farmers who keep up will do better than those who don't. I'd say that to Dad, in a friendly way. Feed, planning and records, and the vet clinic's booking, all go to software, and that frees me up for the animals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good about my degree. Animal science mixes thinking and hands-on, so some of the planning goes to AI but the animals still need me. For the farm, it could lower costs, like using an AI to plan feed rations and spotting a limping ewe from a camera. I'd be excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put what I know to use at home. I'd set up a simple system for the flock records, try a camera for lambing night, and test an AI ration planner on last year's numbers. At the vet clinic I'd suggest we use the tools for booking and reminders. I'd also keep studying, so that I'm the one who understands both the animals and the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Energised, with a bit of impatience. I want to get on and do it, and Dad needs to be talked round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you talk Dad round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How do you talk Dad round?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your brother share your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With numbers. I'd say, give me one field, one season and one tool, and let me show you the difference. Dad can't argue with a cheaper feed bill. He's careful, not stubborn, and he respects results. I'd also take my brother with me, because he'll back me if he sees it works.

say: I'd say it's good news for those who **work with it**; farmers who keep up will do better.
I'd tell Dad, in a friendly way, to **try it**.
think: Animal science mixes thinking and **hands-on**, so planning goes to AI but the animals still need me.
The farm could **lower costs** with a ration planner and a lambing camera.
do: **Set up** a flock records system and test an AI ration planner on last year's numbers.
**Try** a lambing night camera at home.
**Suggest** the vet clinic uses the tools for bookings and reminders.
feel: **Energised** and impatient, with Dad needing to be talked round.
S1.quote: Dad can't argue with a cheaper feed bill. He's careful, not stubborn, and he respects results.
fieldNote: Chloe's **adaptive** side makes her expect gains, so she is calm in this middle case.
She plans to **persuade by pilot**, one field, one season, one tool.
The brother is a **possible ally**, but the succession question stays unspoken.

steps.text: Test an AI ration planner on last year's feed numbers
Set up a camera for lambing night at home
Suggest booking and reminder tools at the vet clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that I'm excited and scared in equal parts, and that the first thing is to protect people on low incomes, because they'll be hit before the rest. I'd say that I don't want handouts for everyone, but I'd want real help getting people into work that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried about the farm. By 2028, thinking work is done by AI, so the clerks, buyers and processors the farm sells to would be hit, and prices could swing. Hands-on farm work lasts until 2031, but the money side of farming is mostly thinking work. And I'd be about to start my third year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go home and work with Dad on the farm's finances, looking for a way to cut costs. I'd learn all I can about AI farm tools, because farms that use them will beat those that don't. I'd save every spare pound and cut my own spending. I'd keep my animal science degree, because the hands-on skills last longest. And I'd talk to my brother about the future of the farm, before things get urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fast-hearted. It's a mix of adrenaline and nerves, like before a race. I'd be pushing hard, and I'd check in with my mum often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What do you say to your brother?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your degree if the farm needs you full time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to my brother, let's stop pretending the farm will just wait for us. Let's agree who does what, and what each of us needs. I'd want to know if he's staying, because if he is, we have to plan for both of us. It's the talk we've been avoiding, and AI just gave us a deadline.

say: I'd say I'm **excited and scared** in equal parts and low earners get hit before the rest.
I'd want **real help** into work that lasts, not handouts for everyone.
think: Clerks, buyers and processors the farm sells to would be hit, and **prices could swing**.
The **money side** of farming is mostly thinking work, even if farm work is hands-on.
do: **Go** home and work with Dad on the farm's finances to cut costs.
**Learn** AI farm tools and save every spare pound.
**Talk** to my brother about the future of the farm.
feel: **Fast-hearted**: adrenaline and nerves, like before a race.
S2.quote: I'd say to my brother, let's stop pretending the farm will just wait for us.
fieldNote: The **farm's cash flow** is what makes her anxious: buyers and processors are thinking-work firms.
The deadline turns a **family avoidance** into an agenda, and she acts on it.
She is **adaptive**: more AI tools, not fewer, is her answer.

steps.text: Go home and work through the farm's finances with Dad
Learn AI farm planning tools in the holidays
Cut my own spending and save every spare pound
Talk to my brother about who takes the farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you're sensible, and I'd say every farm should be using the tools. I'd say it in the farming group chat, and I'd tell friends to build skills that mix biology, animals and technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be cautiously upbeat. I'd graduate in 2029, with two years of thinking AI before robots reach farms. The farm has a window to buy a few smart tools and cut costs. Dad is sixty, so he'd be near retirement by 2034, which makes succession the bigger question than AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and use the vet clinic to learn practical skills. I'd help Dad update the farm's records and pilot one or two tools, and save a pot of money to invest in something like a milking robot equivalent for sheep, or a shearing system. I'd also talk with my brother and Dad about who runs what by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. It feels like there's a plan I can make, and I'm good at plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you buy first, with the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you buy first, with the money?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dad's retirement mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd buy for the farm is a good weighing and drafting system, and it pays back in about three years. It cuts the labour and gives us better records. After that, a drone for checking the hill sheep. I'd need to prove the first one before Dad lets me do the second.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if you're sensible, and every farm should use the tools.
I'd tell friends to build skills mixing **biology, animals and technology**.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with **two years** of thinking AI before robots reach farms.
Dad is sixty, so **succession** is a bigger question than AI.
do: **Finish** my degree and use the vet clinic to learn practical skills.
**Pilot** one or two tools on the farm and save for a weighing system.
**Agree** with Dad and my brother who runs what by 2031.
feel: **Good**: there's a plan I can make, and I'm good at plans.
S3.quote: The first thing I'd buy for the farm is a good weighing and drafting system, and it pays back in about three years.
fieldNote: Time lets Chloe turn the farm into a **investment plan**, with an AI-plus-machinery path.
**Succession**, not AI, is the largest question she raises.
She is **cautiously upbeat** but unsettled by the unspoken brother question.

steps.text: Pilot one AI tool on the farm's flock records
Save for a weighing and drafting system
Agree with Dad and my brother who runs what
Finish my degree and keep vet clinic shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, and farms that start now will be well ahead. I'd say to Dad and my brother that this is the decade to change how the farm is run, step by step, without risking the lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel pretty good. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, probably working on the farm or running a vet practice with a farm focus. Dad would be retired and my brother and I would have worked out who does what. I'd be sorry for farms without family to take over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my degree, and then a year or two at a big vet practice or an agricultural consultancy to learn the business. I'd bring those ideas home and phase in tools one at a time. I'd also invest in good land or kit when I can. And I'd write down the family plan with my brother, with a lawyer, so it's fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Maybe a bit like a kid with a new toolkit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair plan with your brother look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would a fair plan with your brother look like?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone sceptical about AI on farms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One that doesn't depend on who shouts louder. We might split the farm into the sheep side and the arable side, or one of us buys the other out over time. I'd want the family plan written before Dad retires, because the family arguments that follow retirements are the worst. I've seen it happen to our neighbours.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** and farms that start now will be well ahead.
I'd tell Dad and my brother to change the farm **step by step**.
think: By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, on the farm or running a **farm-focused vet practice**.
Dad would be retired, and my brother and I would have **settled** who does what.
do: **Work** a year or two at a vet practice or agricultural consultancy.
**Phase in** one tool at a time on the family farm.
**Write down** a fair family plan with my brother and a lawyer.
feel: **Excited**, like a kid with a new toolkit.
S4.quote: I'd want the family plan written before Dad retires, because the family arguments that follow retirements are the worst.
fieldNote: With a decade, Chloe is **calm** and her plan turns to fairness between siblings.
She cites **neighbours' arguments** as the reason to write things down.
Her **adaptive** style is step by step, not leap by leap.

steps.text: Work at a vet practice or consultancy for a year or two
Phase in one farm tool at a time
Write a fair family farm plan with my brother

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the farm's money and the family talk both need more time than that. What would help is practical training in the tools for farmers, fair prices from buyers, and decent rural broadband. And a family plan, written down, before things get pressured.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that farm kids aren't behind on technology. A lot of us use it every day, and we also know what it costs to get a lamb through a bad night.

headlineQuote: Farm kids aren't behind on technology. A lot of us use it every day, and we also know what it costs to get a lamb through a bad night.
portrait: Chloe is **nineteen**, an animal science student who works vet clinic reception and goes home to the family sheep farm.
She is **traditional** and adaptive, using AI tools every day and believing in work, family and step-by-step investment.
Her biggest pressure is the farm's **thin margin** and an unspoken question about who takes over.
She is uneasy in slow worlds, **anxious** at two years, and calm when a decade gives her time to plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because the farm's money and the family talk need more time.
whatWouldHelp: Practical **training** in tools for farmers, fair buyer prices, good rural broadband and a written family plan.
